I am a 51-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, and I have worked this land for 35 years. My farm is 16.9 mu, just me and my wife at home now—our children work off-farm in the city. With only two of us, I have to be smart about labor. I have a well for irrigation, which is my advantage when the rains do not cooperate. I know this soil like the back of my hand.

For my **winter wheat**, I will plant the full 16.9 mu in October after rotary tillage. I use an improved variety that performs well here—hybrid wheat is not common in our village, and I save some seed from year to year, but I also buy fresh seed when the old batch weakens. Before sowing, I spread compound fertilizer as a base dressing, and at green-up or jointing I topdress with urea. All together, I put down about 18 kg of nitrogen, 7 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu. I irrigate four times: once before winter to help the crop survive the cold, once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling if the weather turns dry. I spray herbicide once after sowing, and I keep an eye out for aphids and powdery mildew—usually two more sprays handle it. I expect about 520 kg per mu if the weather holds.

For **summer maize**, I plant immediately after wheat harvest in early June. Time is short, so I do not till—I sow directly into the wheat stubble. I use hybrid seed; everyone here does, because the yield difference is too big to ignore. At sowing, I put down fertilizer with the seeder, and when the plants reach the big trumpet stage I topdress with more nitrogen. Total nutrients are about 14 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate twice: once if the seedling stage is dry, and the critical one at silking. For pests, I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice for corn borer. I expect around 580 kg per mu.

This is the system that has fed my family for decades, and I see no reason to change it.
